title: Baby Brains - Nature vs. Nurture, Not So Simple
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the third of seven and a half lessons on the brain from Dr. Lisa Feldman Barrett's book, here on how baby brains develop and why nature versus nurture is too small a frame. Nomon describes infants starting with twice as many neurons as adults, then being tuned and pruned by caregivers who regulate the physical environment and share attention, as when a mother looks at a toy dog, then at the baby, then back. The Romanian orphanages under Ceaușescu show what happens without that care. A New York Times article on the Baby's First Years study, which gives poor mothers monthly cash cards, leads Nomon to a Family Promise exercise with Smarties candies standing in for a family's resources.

We try to notice that there's this opportunity to do activities differently than our usual striving way, where we're trying to do everything perfectly, not make any mistakes, and thinking that if we do, it shows that we're a bad person.
Just showing up and doing our best is right.
Karen couldn't have done that wrong, but that was awesome, great job Karen.

If you'd like to take a stab at that, Talus has put together a little instrument kit, so he will even deliver it to you.
I understand we're working on training materials, and several people will be happy to practice with you on Zoom.

Well, let's dive back into a little mix of brain science and Buddhist psychology tonight, mostly brain science, but this brain science I realized has some really important implications for us in our bodhisattva aspiration, our bodhisattva work in the third lesson, lesson number three of seven and a half lessons on a brain.
Dr.

Barrett talks about how young brains develop according to this more current neuroscience, which I'm sure she greatly simplified for us, but I really have a lot of faith in what she's saying is very accurate to the scientific field, really current.

One thing is that it turns out that the old nature versus nurture idea in the development of humans—this huge idea that we hear all the time, is it your genetics or your environment, is it your nature or your nurture—that idea doesn't really make sense anymore from the perspective of modern neuroscience.
The ideas implied by nature and nurture are off from reality, she says.
In terms of nature, genes don't work the way we're assuming they do.
When we say stuff like that, they aren't like this fixed blueprint that sets you on a very particular developmental direction from birth or from conception.
Genes are important for sure; they regulate the creation of cells and so on, what kind of cells and how many, and all this.
We each have our own unique combination of genetic material from our parents and so on, but genes are not like propensities.
How they express and how they influence development is conditional and causal, and influenced by a million other factors, many of them are environmental, and it's not even all your genes.

Some of you know our sangha sister Lee Nelson, who's also a researcher in human development, and she's made some important discoveries that after birth, some of the mother's genetic material cruises back through the umbilical cord and affects the fetus as it's born or maybe before, I forget.
In the book, she barely mentions and doesn't explain that there may also be genetic material from various microbes in us, governing our development.
So nature is not so simple as, "that kid had that blueprint and ended up this way, and that kid had that blueprint and ended up that way."
And the nurture piece isn't right either because the idea is implied from nature in nature versus nurture; they are just way too small, not nearly big enough.
How we're nurtured and we learn in this book is not just a kind of psychological good or bad influences or culture, although certainly those are important.
It turns out how we're nurtured—exactly, the exact actions that happen in your nurturing—actually regulate the way your actual brain develops.
So nurture is huge in a much bigger topic than what it sounds like in nature versus nurture.
They're both a little off because it turns out the environment children grow up in doesn't just sort of affect what's sort of like inside their brains.

We have this idea that there's stuff inside our brains—knowledge and skills—but actually the environment and the nurturing children receive helps to govern and affect the very structure and function of the brain.

Since the brain's big job is maintaining our life, maintaining a healthy allostasis, that also means that a body in which the brain doesn't get enough of the proper kind of nurturing and doesn't develop right leads to a body that doesn't develop right either.
They're not separate at all.

A little sidebar here because I think we have all these persistent beliefs that I'm learning, maybe you agree with me, or maybe you're learning too, or maybe already knew, but all these beliefs about what our brain is and how it works and how the mind works, and a lot of them are wrong.
How is it hard to even know all the ways that affect how we think, how we interact, how we perceive ourselves, how we conceive of the world?
What I was thinking here was just the idea that brains have thoughts in them, that they have contents that are separate from some sort of function and structure.
That's wrong.

The structure and function of the brain at this neural level, this massive network, is generating all of our experiences—our thoughts, our memories, our perceptions, our sense of space in the body—it's all being generated by this functional network all the time, in real time.
And this network is constantly changing around, so it made me realize that another model we have of our brain is that our brain is like a computer.
One shouldn't even bother to refute that one.

She worked on other models in the book in the earlier chapters, but sometimes we think that the brain is the hardware, and the thinking and the emotions and the culture and all that stuff is like the software.
But the reality seems to be far more intertwined than that, far more rich and complex than the reality of our brain.
If we were to upgrade the software, it causes the hardware to reorganize itself and rewire itself.
The mouse and the computer and the keyboard and the chips all flip around and change; it's all one system in the same, in the other direction.
If you were to change the hardware, it changes the software, so that doesn't really work either.
The thing that's relevant for tonight is that what pops out of the uterus is not like a computer that rolls out of the factory fully assembled and ready to boot up.
Maybe it needs some software installed, learn how to be a person software, but no, it's this malleable, fluid, changing dynamic system, cause and effect just at a million levels.
Anyway, back to baby brains.

The surprising thing to me to learn among many things here is that baby brains start out with an even more massive network of neurons than we end up with as adults, she says, about twice as many neurons.
We already end up with something like a hundred twenty-five billion neurons; you start with twice that in this teeny little infant brain.
It's unbelievable, and it's kind of counterintuitive.
Why would you start with too much?
We would tend to think that you would start with less, right?
You'd start with a simple network because you're small and that you would gradually elaborate and grow more, but it turns out it works in the other direction.
This massive starter set of neural network of stuff is pruned and tuned and optimized to become an adult brain, sculpted and shaped by experience.
This tuning and pruning, this development, is not automatic, like I was saying.
It's not like a pre-programmed direction.

There is development, there is directionality in it, but it's not a single path because it's so responsive to the experiences the baby has—not just what they learn, but how the brain ends up structured and how it functions.

Just like we were talking about last week with neuroplasticity, that the brain can make fast or somewhat slower changes through neural changes in the structure as you learn new stuff, that's just going at high speed with babies.

The most important, she says, and primary experiences that are happening in this development—no surprise, really—but the mechanism really gives us more weight, but the most important thing that's going on is the loving, sustained, engaged contact with the baby's caregivers, with the parents for whoever's raising the baby.
If that doesn't happen, the brain does not develop not very well at all, so it's not automatic at all.
The other thing she reminds us about in this chapter, which is worth remembering, I think, is that we are pretty weird compared to other animals in terms of how helpless our newborns are.
Horses and giraffes can walk after a couple of days, she pointed out.
Newborn chimps are strong and dexterous enough to hold on to their mama's back.
Brand new newborn snakes can slither along just fine, but newborn humans can't do much of anything.
All they can really do is wriggle towards the smell of breast milk.
What that's like, what little ability they start with, that's it.
They can't control their limbs, direct their eyesight, or do much of anything when they're born.
This is so normal to us that newborns are that way, kind of helpless, but it's just because we're used to it.
It's actually like really weird, really unusual in the animal world.
So there must be then that there's some kind of big advantage to this.

I mean, evolution is not deliberate like that, but there must be some evolutionary advantage for us to end up that way with this really slow period of development, and the advantage must have to do with having lots of time to slowly develop this brain.

Having decades, depending on how you count it—ten years, eighteen years, twenty years, twenty-five—to develop our brain, it must end up with humans as really evolutionarily fit, really great, because other species have a lot of the stuff that we spend our initial years developing just baked in, but we don't have that.
Instead, we have this kind of blank slate, which ends up being a very high potential system.
The potential is only actualized though because of other adult humans that are around; that's the only way it can be actualized.
It can only be a collective social project to develop new humans to end up with something so amazing as you, as me.
But the thing is, there's a downside to that kind of potential and to this dependence on human society to help humans become fully humans.
It's not at birth, it's not just at birth, it's not just genetics.
The downside or the risk or the area of body self for work for our culture and our society and our species is then we can get a huge amount of disparity.
We can get very uneven amounts of this secondary development that's so critical.
Some babies, as you know, get lots of great caregiving and support, and some don't, and this has a lifetime effect and a multi-generational effect.
So there's a lot of potential, but there's also a lot of potential for a kind of unhappy sorting of individuals and societal groups.

Sadly, as I think all of us are learning more and more clearly, and other groups involved have known for generations and generations, a lot of that sorting happens between groups that we arbitrarily label as races, and some races, which is not a biological anything, it's a cultural idea, tend to get more and some tend to get less.
So this is I think part of why this is really important to have at least the elementary school level of neuroscience this book is giving us.
The way the neurological workings happen is pretty interesting; the brain starts out, as I said, with twice as many neurons as we end up with, a massive starter set packed in there.
and then experiences cause those neurons to fire up and interact in different intricate patterns that leads to what she calls tuning and pruning.
I am trying to remember that she is massively simplifying the science, and there is probably nothing in scientific literature called tuning and pruning, but she is helping us out.
Tuning is a strengthening of connections between neurons, neural pathways.
They get used a lot and therefore must be important.
If they are getting used a lot, they become more efficient.
As we learned last week, it is already more complicated than our brains are thinking because we are so mechanically minded.
We think of neuronal pathways like one pathway, or sometimes they talk about the wiring of the brain, like there are little copper wires running around, but no, this is a superorganic system.
We learned that one particular neuron does not do the same thing over and over again.
Different neighboring neurons take turns, and they cluster, and they cooperate, and they trade off, and they switch around.
It is a very has a lot of redundancy and complexity, and what she called degeneracy in the system.
But collectively, in loose units of neurons, there is this increase in efficiency in parts of the brain; they are getting used more.
Sometimes they call all this neurons that fire together wire together, and this happens through the very structure of these neurons.
It is really cool.
So the neurons are getting used more, get more of this bushy stuff at the end of each end of the little trunk, like stock called dendrites.
At the end of those dendrites are neurotransmitters.

Those neurotransmitters remember the ones that secrete little neurochemicals and talk to the and therefore through this chemical handoff, trigger their neighboring neurons and do kind of a communication.
We call it communication, and they do not have that word for it, right?
They do not have that way of thinking, but it is this intricate functioning.
So there is this tuning that systems they used a lot get more efficient, which is good, you know, because we also remember trying to balance all the metabolic needs of this animal.
If one system uses up way too much, we will be tired all the time; we will have to eat constantly, you know, be unhealthy for us.
So from the beginning, the brain works on how can I be more efficient.
One of those ways is tuning.
The other thing that happens in the tuning, besides the richer dendrites at the end of areas that need to connect more often, is the very electrical signal runs faster and more strongly.
Partly because there is a kind of sheath around that central axon called myelin, like insulation, like bark on a tree trunk, that allows that electrical signal to work better.
Sometimes brains have trouble with any one of these processes, and one of ones that brains are likely to have trouble with is growing enough myelin in the right places.
If your brain has trouble with that, then you have all kinds of problems.
But anyway, most of us have habit, it is fine.
So that is tuning.
But if the brain's baby's brain starts out with twice as many neurons as we end up with, something else has to happen, and that is pruning.
That sounds kind of awful, you know, why would we want to lose a lot of brain cells?
We were told earlier in our education that you only have so many, you know, don't lose any.
But this is just so again, so the brain can be more efficient.
Neurons and patterns that are not being used tend to draw and die off, and so this is really healthy and essential.
Or those neurons become simpler with fewer dendrites and fewer neuroreceptors.
So there is this process happening, but how does it, why does it happen?
What is it responding to?
Since the brain changes in response to experience and response to what is happening, so here we have we are back to caregiving.
She gives examples of how the baby's environment affects this process into two big categories: the physical environment and the social environment.
Experiences, good and bad in either environment, have a huge effect on the development of the brain and are hugely affected by the caregiver adults in the baby's life.
They take actions, and those actions affect the development of the brain.
The actions in the physical environment surprise me, and she talks about it this way that when we adults need to do something to take care of ourselves, like we are hungry, we can get food, right?
We know how to do that.
When we are tired, we can go to bed.
When we are cold, we put on our fleece because we are in the northwest, we turn up the thermostat, and we already have this ability to do that.
So our brain does not have to use a lot of resources to maintain our nutrition, our rest, and our energy, right?
So our brain can take care of other things.
We know how to put on a sweater, you know, and that is only because of all these years of development that that is easy for our brain to do.
And our brains then have resources left to do all the other crazy things that humans can do: sing songs, compose way too many emails, listen to dharma talks.

But if we were really stressed out right now, all of us, about how to even cope with our physical environment, if we did not understand how to do all these things that we do without thinking about it, you would not be able to focus on my words right now.
You would be busy trying to navigate how can I stay warm and fed and happy and okay, right?
You already know how to do that.
So you have these other things you can do with your brain, but babies cannot do any of this, and that is where the caregivers come in.
But this is the trip about this took me a while to kind of think this through.

The caregiver is not just keeping the baby fed and warm so that the baby can develop; they are actually facilitating brain development in the area of relating to the environment that the caregivers are regulating the baby's physical environment enough that the baby is kind of within its healthy sort of developmental lane and can develop without too much stress.

So even though you put the onesie on the baby and tuck in the blankets in the crib, the baby is still going to get a little chilly, and so its brain has to learn how to manipulate metabolism to keep things at the right temperature internally.
If you did not do any of that, then the brain would have a much bigger job, so much harder for it to develop something like metabolic balance.
Same thing with food, you know.
The baby has to learn how to respond to hunger and understand the signals that represent hunger; that is a whole complicated thing, and then it has to figure out how to get food, right?
Which in this case means learning the right kind of fussing.
They will be interpreted by your caregivers as, "I'm hungry, feed me, please."

But here too, the caregiver most does most of the heavy lifting by thinking, "Oh, the baby might be hungry, you know," or "You know, it is about dinner time, let's feed the baby," so the baby has much less stress as it works all this stuff out and develops how to interact with the physical environment.
So isn't that interesting?

Caregivers are not just keeping the baby fed and warm and in diapers; they are actually facilitating this gradual ability to manage and cope with a physical body in a physical world, which is a very complicated thing to do even with all our modern conveniences.
We are just used to it.
And so you can imagine what happens if that does not happen.
So that is the physical sphere of caregiving.
The social sphere of caregiving is also super important, which is no surprise.
But a really cool example she gives of this is the development of attention, and we all know from our own practice and from everyday life how utterly essential attention is, right?
You know, to be able to actually to in large part control and direct our attention.
If we could not do that, we would be utterly lost, right?
Lost in a sea of sensory and mental information, we would be bewildered beyond belief, and we are not because we are we learned how not to be, you know, and now we do that more or less automatically.

And of course, our ability to work with our attention is far from perfect, which is one of the things that we so much shockingly find out usually when we start meditation, you know, and are reminded of every time we sit down, "Oh my gosh, my attentional control is definitely imperfect," right?
You know, I know perfectly well my intention is to sit and breathe and be still, and here I am, you know, planning what I am going to do after retirement, you know, holy smokes.
But actually, we are pretty darn good if you consider the intensity of that problem that an unbelievable amount of information is flowing in through all the senses and through the thinking mind.
The brain has to navigate, and somehow we are able to choose pretty much what to attend to, with some distraction sure.
But babies cannot do any of this, right?
And the way she talks about this is this that babies do not know what is important and what is not.
How could they know?
Knowing that does not come in the so-called genetic code because the brain is this unformed massive network, so they cannot focus as adults do.
They lack the wiring to narrow their broad attention; they start with a very broad attention, which she likens to a lantern just shining light in all directions, you know.
And you know that is beautiful too, right?
We love the way babies just soak it in, right?
Wow, you know.
And we are into the downside of our selective attention also, so there are pros and cons here.
Maybe with our practice, we are trying to end up with some of both, I do not know, or we are ignoring the beautiful sky because we are worried about work or whatever.

So we have ways of narrowing our attention that are not always the best too, but anyway, just in terms of functioning in the world and staying alive, which is the main function of the organism, babies do not know and do not yet know how to do this attentional part.
And this essential ingredient comes from caregivers in the social world, so this is huge actually.
The caregivers constantly guide the baby's attention to things of interest.
Her example was a mother picks up a toy dog and looks at it, and she looks at the baby, and back at the dog, and what she is doing is actually guiding the baby's gaze with her modeling.
It is a process they called shared attention, so she is sharing her attentional regulation with the baby.
Language development happens right along with it, you know.
She turns to the kid and says very intentionally, "What a cute doggy," right?
And the mother's speech and the back and forth switching of gaze and all of it adds up to this powerful developmental process.

So playing with the baby is not just kind of cute and fun and nice to do; it is actually facilitating neurological development in a very direct way because little by little this shared attention teaches an infant which parts of the vast environment matter and which parts do not, and the brain is sculpted as a result.
Tuning and pruning happen, the software and the hardware evolve, which is all very cool.

But then we come back to this social justice angle and all this because when a baby grows up in an environment where there is not enough of this caregiving assistance in learning to develop their understanding of the physical and social world, then there is trouble.
In the book, she gives the horrible example which I had forgotten about, I remember reading about it ages ago, but I had forgotten about this.

This was not long ago either, the example from Romania where the dictator, you know, President Nicolae Ceaușescu, wanted to expand the population of Romania so there would be more workers for the factories, so he banned birth control, led to a glut of babies in an impoverished society, lots of babies the families could not afford to take care of.
And then he figured out what to do about that; he created a system of large orphanages, hundreds of thousands of children.

It is just a crushing number; it is hard to really let it even get into your head, you know, hundreds of thousands of babies in these large warehousey orphanages, and in the orphanages the caregivers could only attend
Just the very basic, most basic of physical needs, the very minimum to keep the babies going, which maybe the organizers of this system thought was all the babies really needed.
The caregivers going down rows of cribs to feed, change, and clothe babies, but no time to cuddle them or talk to them or give them the care babies really need.
The social environment was minimal, and the social environment was just an utter desert, really horrid to think about.
This generation, these many, many people grew up intellectually impaired, she said, especially they had really low impulse control and stunted bodies too, right?
The brain's trying to do the allostatic regulation as the body grows, and if it can't do that, the body doesn't grow, right?
So, a horrible example of how this process can go wrong.
But I think also maybe a little bit too easy for us to say, "Well, that's history, and somewhere else, you know, maybe it's over and done with, we know better now."
But in our own society, our own country, we have the intertwined racial economic disparities that basically lead to another version of the exact same thing.
Dr.

Barrett didn't mention this in her book that white middle-class babies are just much more likely than poor black or brown babies to get the environment and the social caregiving their brains need to develop well, and it's not for lack of love of the parents or anything like that.
It's not for want of trying, for sure; it's structural, it's economical, it's economic, it's environmental, and it's deeply multi-generational.
Surprisingly, I ran into a New York Times article just a couple of days ago that talks about this.

It's talking about some research into this, which is really interesting, and I think important, and also that it's reminding us, if you didn't catch this detail of the massive Biden economic relief plan, that it includes financial support for low-income families with children.

And the article points out—I'm going to read a little chunk of it in a moment—that this is not just like a nice thing, you know, to give the families a leg up, you know, reduce this or that social problem for them, but it could actually improve brain development and therefore human development and a whole segment of our society.
This could have positive, kind of upward spiral effects, you know, for generations if we could keep doing this.
Here's the article, really part of it: "It's well established that growing up in poverty correlates with disparities in educational achievement, health, and employment.
But emerging brands of neuroscience asks how poverty affects the developing brain.

Over the past fifteen years, dozens of studies have found that children raised in meager circumstances have subtle but important brain differences compared with children from families of higher means.

On average, for example, the surface area of the brain's outer layer of cells is smaller, especially in areas related to language and impulse control, as is the volume of a structure called the hippocampus, which is responsible for learning and memory."
Well, side bar, that's back to the very simple language that one part of the brain just does one thing, but that's okay.
It mostly goes on these differences don't reflect inherited or inborn traits.
Research suggests nature versus nurture, but rather the circumstances in which the children grew up.

Researchers have speculated that specific aspects of poverty—subpar nutrition, elevated stress levels, lower quality education—might influence brain and cognitive development, but almost all the work to date is correlational.
I was looking for connections, don't know how it happens, and although these factors may be at play to various degrees for differing families, poverty is their common route.
A continuing study called Baby's First Year started in 2018 aims to determine whether reducing poverty can help promote healthy brain development.
"None of us thinks income is the only answer," said Dr.
Kimberly Nobel, a neuroscientist and pediatrician at Teachers College, Columbia University, which is co-leading the work.
"The Baby's First Years with Baby's First Years, we are moving past correlation to test whether reducing poverty directly causes changes in children's cognition, emotional, and brain development."
Dr.

Nobel and her collaborators are examining the effects of giving poor families cash payments in amounts that wound up being comparable to those of the Biden administration that the Biden administration will distribute as part of an expanded child tax credit.
So, it's a trippy thing; this research was already giving families about the same amount, and Biden comes along and says, "We're going to do that for everybody."

The researchers randomly assigned one thousand mothers with newborns living in poverty in New York City, New Orleans, the Twin Cities, in Omaha to receive a debit card every month holding either twenty dollars or three hundred thirty-three dollars that the families could deal with as they wished, the Biden plans about three hundred.

The study tracks cognitive development and brain activity in these children over several years and using a non-invasive tool called a mobile EEG, which measures brain wave patterns using a wearable cap of twenty electrons.

The study also tracks the mother's financial and employment status, maternal health measures such as stress hormone levels, sorry, and childcare use, and in qualitative interviews, the researchers probe how the money affects the family and with the mother's consent, they follow how they choose to spend the money.

The study aimed to collect brain activity data from children age one to age three in home visits, and the researchers managed to obtain the first set of data for about two-thirds of the children before the pandemic struck because home visits are still untenable.
They extended the study to age four.
We'll be collecting a second set of brain data next year instead of this year.

The pandemic as well as the two stimulus payments most Americans received this past year undoubtedly affected participating families in different ways as well this year—stimulus checks and new monthly payments.
But the study is now randomized, so the researchers nonetheless hope to be able to assess the impacts of the cash gift.
In the study Baby's First Year is seen as an audacious effort to prove through a randomized trial a causal link between poverty reduction and brain development.

"It is definitely one of the first, if not the first, study in this developing field to have direct policy implications," and that one of the researchers concedes, "you know, there's a lot we don't know."
She said, "Are there actionable insights we will get by bringing neuroscience to bear, or people just being snowed by pretty brain images and impressive sounding words from neuroscience?"
It's an important question, so they want to be careful, you know, how solid are the results and how are they interpreted?

Isn't that wild, you know, that the best intervention for helping children in poverty could be simply to give a family three hundred bucks a month that could change lives, you know, forever and change our society?

The other thing I think is really interesting about this study, and a real change from maybe some earlier attitudes about assistance programs and stuff, is they leave it up to the mother to decide how to spend the money, and so they'll see a lot from those choices as well because they don't really know which exact aspects of the environment are affecting these babies, you know, will it help if the most if they have better food, less toxic products, safer neighborhood, better schools?
Is it down to more basic survival stuff, like enough money for heating, you know, clothes, and so on?
And that made me think about a training that we did for the Family Promise program.
Our song is a part of that, helps homeless families with food and shelter in Bellingham.
In the training, they gave us a little chart of basic needs to put little tokens on.

The tokens were actually Smarties candies, you know, come as little rolls, little sugar candies, little disks, and we got the starter set of some number of tokens that represent resources, represent money, and we had just enough tokens to pay for all the basic needs just barely—things like heating, daycare, clothing, food, cell phone, transportation.
